content_voiceover: This diagram shows where fibrinolysis actually begins, right at the vessel wall. The endothelial cells lining the blood vessel are shown releasing two key activators. Pointing upward, they release tissue plasminogen activator, or t-PA, which is the main driver of fibrinolysis. Pointing down into the forming thrombus, they also release u-PA, the urokinase-type plasminogen activator. In the middle of the vessel you can see a cross-section of a developing thrombus: a meshwork of polymerized fibrin strands that has trapped a neutrophil and several red blood cells. So even as the clot is forming and trapping cellular elements, the neighboring endothelium is simultaneously priming the fibrinolytic system to eventually break that clot down. This is the physiologic basis for why thrombi are not permanent, healthy endothelium is constantly working to limit and eventually dissolve them.
keypoints: Endothelial cells release t-PA, the main driver of fibrinolysis
Endothelial cells also release u-PA locally into the thrombus
The thrombus is a fibrin meshwork trapping neutrophils and red cells
Fibrinolysis is initiated right at the site of clot formation
keypoint_voiceover: To recap, the vessel wall's endothelial cells release t-PA and u-PA, the two plasminogen activators, right at the site where fibrin, trapped neutrophils, and red cells have formed a thrombus, setting up fibrinolysis from the very start.
